chapter_theme: Manimekalai takes refuge in the three jewels and her teacher expounds dependent arising: the twelve links forward and in reverse, with their four sections, three junctions, three times, the four truths, the five aggregates, the modes of speech, the four nayas and the four ways of answering, ending in the claim that bondage and release have their own causes and no giver, and in a remedy for each of desire, anger and delusion; hearing it, she vows to end the round of becoming. The kaathai is the Buddhist doctrine the debates of kaathai 27 were set aside for.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, now a Buddhist renunciant hearing the doctrine
the Buddhist teacher who expounds the doctrine; named in this kaathai only as மொழிவோன்
the Buddha, whose descent, awakening and teaching the discourse recounts

manimekalai:30:1-6.unit_note: Boundary moved from 17 to 6: lines 1-6 are the narrator's frame, closing on மொழிவோன் (line 6); the teacher's speech opens at line 7, and the core unit 1-17 ran the frame into the middle of the speech.
manimekalai:30:1-6.reading: Manimekalai, who has known what she entered into in her former birth by holding to giving and keeping the precepts, bows three times to the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha and goes to them for refuge, and the teacher begins to speak the form of dharma.
manimekalai:30:1-6.nuance: தானம் and சீலம் (line 1) are the two practices she held in her former birth, and the same pair returns at line 78 as what makes a good birth: the teacher's doctrine of good deeds is first shown in the hearer. The teacher is only மொழிவோன், 'the one who speaks'; the story so far makes him Aravana Adigal.
manimekalai:30:1-6.event: Manimekalai takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, and the teacher begins his discourse.

manimekalai:30:7-33.unit_note: Boundary moved from 17/18 to 6/7: the speech that begins at line 7 is now one unit up to the core boundary at 33, ending on the list of the chain's properties.
manimekalai:30:7-33.reading: The teacher says that when the world's knowledge had run dry the Buddha came down from the Tushita heaven at the gods' entreaty, sat at the Bodhi tree, conquered Mara and taught, as countless past Buddhas taught, the twelvefold teaching of arising by dependence: where this is not that is not, where this is that is, with four sections, three junctions, three modes and three times, the ground of the four truths and the account of the five aggregates.
manimekalai:30:7-33.nuance: Lines 21-22 (ஈங்கு இது இல்லாவழி இல்லாகி / ஈங்கு இது உள்ளவழி உண்டு ஆகலின்) give the general formula of dependence before any of the twelve is named. The long run of ஆகி and உடைத்தாய் from line 16 is a table of contents for the whole kaathai: each item (sections, junctions, times, truths, aggregates, modes of speech, nayas, kinds of answer) is expounded later in this order.

claims.claim: all the Buddhas of past ages taught one and the same truth
things arise in dependence: where this is not, that is not; where this is, that is
seeing fault, deed and fruit as unstable, empty and suffering is the sure way to release

manimekalai:30:34-58.reading: The teacher says the chain has no maker and is not made, has no I and no mine, no going and no coming, and is itself deed, fruit, birth and release; he names the twelve links, ignorance, action, consciousness, name-and-form, the six gates, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth and the fruit of deeds, says that those who know them gain the great reward and those who do not know hell, and defines ignorance as forgetting what reasoning has shown and trusting the report that a hare has horns, before naming the six kinds of beings.
manimekalai:30:34-58.nuance: Line 37 (நின்மதி இன்றி ஊழ்பாடு இன்றி) is compressed: I read it as 'without a governing mind and without fixed fate', but நின்மதி may be read otherwise, and the tension link to the Ajivika rests on ஊழ்பாடு. Ignorance is defined not as plain not-knowing but as preferring hearsay (கேட்டது) to what has been established (கண்டது), with the hare's horn (முயற்கோடு) as the stock example of a non-thing; the same example returns at lines 208 and 216.

claims.claim: the chain of dependent arising has no maker and no fixed fate
in the chain there is no I and nothing that is mine
those who know the twelve links gain the great reward; those who do not know them fall to hell
ignorance is forgetting what reasoning has established and holding as clear what is only heard, as that a hare has horns
living beings are of six kinds: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts

manimekalai:30:59-83.reading: The teacher says that beings enter the womb by good or bad deeds and that the deed's fruit gives them joy or sorrow; he names the ten bad deeds (killing, theft and lust of the body; lying, slander, harsh and idle words of speech; coveting, anger and wrong view of the mind), says those who do them are born as animals, ghosts and hell-beings, and those who avoid them, keep the precepts and give are born as gods, humans and Brahmas; then he defines consciousness as awareness like a sleeper's, without intention or grasp of objects.
manimekalai:30:59-83.nuance: The ten are sorted by where they arise: the body, speech and the mind (உள்ளம் தன்னின் உருப்பன, line 71), so coveting, anger and wrong view count as deeds before any act. Lines 82-83 begin the definitions of the twelve links in the middle of the unit; the address ஆய் தொடி நல்லாய் (line 65) is the teacher's only word to his hearer in the doctrinal part.

claims.claim: beings come to the womb by good or bad deeds, and the ripening deed brings joy or sorrow
the bad deeds are ten: three of the body, four of speech and three of the mind
those who do the ten bad deeds are born as animals, ghosts and hell-beings
those who avoid them, keep the precepts and give are born as gods, humans and Brahmas

manimekalai:30:84-108.reading: The teacher defines the rest of the links: name-and-form as the life and body that go with consciousness, the six gates as the place where contact happens, contact as mind and gate meeting objects, feeling as tasting them, craving as unsated wanting, clinging as sticky knowing, becoming as the heap of karma, birth as appearing in a destiny by that karma, and sickness, aging and death; then he begins the forward chain, each link arising with the one before as its support.
manimekalai:30:84-108.nuance: Death is defined as the name-and-form vanishing like the setting sun (lines 102-103), with யாக்கை as the body that falls: no self passes on. Line 106 spells the link அரூரு where every other line has அருஉரு.

claims.claim: becoming is the accumulation of karma
each link arises with the one before it as its support: ignorance supports action, action consciousness, and so on

manimekalai:30:109-124.reading: The teacher completes the forward chain (contact gives feeling, feeling craving, craving clinging, clinging the heap of karma, and that the next birth, from which come aging, sickness, death, grief, lament, care and despair, an unending sorrow) and then turns to the reverse: as ignorance ceases, action ceases, and so on link by link.
manimekalai:30:109-124.nuance: Line 118 calls the round ஊழின் மண்டிலம், the circle of ஊழ்: the word that elsewhere names fate here names the turning of the chain itself, which line 37 said has no fixed fate.

claims.claim: from birth come aging, sickness, death, grief, lament, care and despair, an unending sorrow
when ignorance ceases action ceases, and each later link ceases with the one before

manimekalai:30:125-138.reading: The teacher finishes the reverse chain, in which birth and all its sorrow cease, and then begins the four sections: the first is this cessation, the second ignorance and action as the causes, and the third begins with consciousness.
manimekalai:30:125-138.nuance: The reverse chain has தோற்றம் and பிறப்பு as two steps (lines 129-130), where the list at lines 45-47 has twelve links with தோற்றம் as the eleventh; the edition's text may double a link here.

claims.claim: by the reverse of the chain all sorrow without end ceases

manimekalai:30:139-154.reading: The teacher completes the four sections (consciousness to feeling, as results of what went before; craving, clinging and becoming, as fault and deed; birth, sickness, aging and death, as the suffering birth brings) and names three junctions: the first awareness of a birth, the knowing of feeling joined with desire, and the karma-heap moving toward the next birth; then he begins the three kinds of birth.
manimekalai:30:139-154.nuance: The junctions (சந்தி) at lines 148-152 are the hinges between the sections, but lines 149-150 (புகர்ச்சி இன்று அறிவது) and 154 are hard to construe, and I cannot fix the second junction's sense beyond the joining of feeling and desire.

claims.claim: craving, clinging and becoming are the fault and the deed within the course of feeling

manimekalai:30:155-169.reading: The teacher gives three kinds of birth (appearing with awareness alone, as form with awareness hidden, and with awareness and form together as humans, gods and animals) and then the three times: ignorance and action belong to the past, consciousness through becoming to the present, and birth with its sorrows to the future; the last line introduces fault.
manimekalai:30:155-169.nuance: Each time-label stands before its list: இறந்த காலம் (160) before ignorance and action, நிகழ்ந்த காலம் (162) before consciousness to becoming, எதிர்காலம் (166) before birth and its sorrows; read the other way, the present links would become future. Line 169's குற்றம் opens the next list rather than closing this one. The three births (155-158) are obscure, and line 155's தோன்றல் வீடு எனத் துணிந்து is a reading I cannot fix.

claims.claim: the twelve links fall across three times: past, present and future

manimekalai:30:170-182.reading: The teacher sorts the links into fault (craving, clinging, ignorance), deed (becoming and action) and fruit (consciousness to feeling, birth, aging, sickness, death); seeing that these are sorrow, unstable, and that no thing has a self, is the nature of release; and he names the links from consciousness to despair as the disease.
manimekalai:30:170-182.nuance: எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை (line 177) is the chapter's one plain statement of no-self, and it is placed as what is to be seen for release, not argued against a rival here. Line 182 begins the four truths with நோய், the disease, the medical frame that runs through the epic's name for the Buddha as the physician of birth.

claims.claim: fault, deed and fruit are suffering and unstable, and no thing has a self
seeing them so is the nature of release

manimekalai:30:183-197.reading: The teacher gives the four truths (the disease, its cause in ignorance, action, craving, clinging and becoming, sorrow caused by birth and clinging, and joy that is release caused by not clinging), names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness), and begins the six modes of speech.
manimekalai:30:183-197.nuance: Line 187 (இன்பம் வீடே பற்றிலி காரணம்) names release as joy, so the third and fourth truths are put as a cause and its result, parallel to the first two. The four truths are called வாய்மை, but they are not the virtue of truthfulness, so I have not tagged vaaimai.

claims.claim: the cause of sorrow is birth and clinging; the cause of release, which is joy, is not clinging
what is spoken of as a person is five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness

manimekalai:30:198-213.reading: The teacher explains the modes of speech by example: the collective name (the body; water; a country), the continuity name (seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy), the name stressing one stage (it perishes, it arose, it aged), the joined name (letters together as a word, days together as a month), and four modes of affirming and denying what exists and what does not, as consciousness, the hare's horn and the mind that flashes up like lightning.
manimekalai:30:198-213.nuance: The point of the modes is that names like paddy or month are conventions for collections and continuities, not things in themselves. The examples for the four existence-modes at lines 208-213 are terse, and which example belongs to which mode is my best construal.

claims.claim: names such as paddy or month are conventions for continuities and collections
mind arises and passes like a flash of lightning

manimekalai:30:214-229.reading: The teacher ends the modes of speech (an effect without a cause is the mode of denial resting on what is not, as there is no arising for a hare's horn) and gives the four nayas: oneness (cause and effect seen as one), difference (each felt apart), non-agency (no mind in the cause that intends its effect) and own-nature (paddy seed gives paddy sprout), and begins what is gained from them: that there is nothing but aggregated things.
manimekalai:30:214-229.nuance: The non-agency naya (lines 223-226) says the cause has no intention of producing the effect, which applies the chain's 'no maker' (line 39) to every cause and effect.

claims.claim: an effect does not come without a cause
a cause has no mind that intends its effect
there is nothing but aggregated things

manimekalai:30:230-243.reading: The teacher completes what the four nayas yield (no clinging to things, no doer apart from the doing, effects come from causes, and the middle that is neither this nor not-this) and names the four ways of answering a question, illustrating two: 'what has arisen will perish' is the definite answer, and a question whether the dead man will be reborn is answered by asking whether he was free of clinging.
manimekalai:30:230-243.unit_note: Boundary moved from 244 to 243: the illustration of the analytic answer ends at விளம்புவர் (line 243), and the example of setting a question aside begins at line 244.
manimekalai:30:230-243.nuance: The rebirth question (lines 240-242) is not answered yes or no but turned to the condition: whether one is reborn depends on whether clinging has ended, which is the chain applied to a person.

claims.claim: there is no doer apart from the doing
whatever has arisen will perish
whether a dead man is reborn depends on whether he has ended clinging

manimekalai:30:244-264.unit_note: Boundary moved from 244/245 to 243/244: line 244 begins the example of setting a question aside (the egg and the palmyra), which runs to 246.
manimekalai:30:244-264.reading: The teacher illustrates the last two kinds of answer (the question whether egg or palmyra came first set aside by asking 'which egg, which palmyra?', and silence before a question about the age of a sky-flower), says bondage and release have their own causes and no one can grant them, names desire, anger and delusion as the cause of all he has taught, and prescribes a remedy for each: seeing impermanence, sorrow, no-self and impurity to cut clinging, friendliness, compassion and sympathetic joy to end hatred, and hearing, reflecting, cultivating and seeing to drive off delusion; the narrator says that, the lamp of knowledge shown, Manimekalai took up austerity and vowed to cut the round of becoming.
manimekalai:30:244-264.nuance: Lines 250-251 (கட்டும் வீடும் அதன் காரணத்தது / ஒட்டித் தருதற்கு உரியோர் இல்லை) deny any giver of bondage or release. Line 253's காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் is the same triad, in the same order, as Kural 360; three words fall short of an echo, so it is a link. Line 263 (தவத் திறம் பூண்டு தருமம் கேட்டு) repeats the title of kaathai 29, and line 264 gives this kaathai its title.
manimekalai:30:244-264.event: Having heard the teaching, Manimekalai takes up austerity and vows to end the round of births.

claims.claim: bondage and release arise from their own causes, and no one exists who can grant them
desire, anger and delusion are the cause of all that has been taught
clinging is cut by seeing things as impermanent, sorrowful, selfless and impure; hatred by friendliness, compassion and sympathetic joy; delusion by hearing, reflection, cultivation and insight

links.note: The goddess hails Manimekalai for recovering her former birth at the Buddha's seat; here that knowledge of the former birth, in which she held to giving and the precepts, is what she brings to her taking of refuge.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show that the memory of a former birth is not the end of her awakening but its qualification: what she recovered on Manipallavam is cashed here as the two practices that make her fit to take refuge and hear the doctrine.

links.note: Aravanar told her that events would happen in the town because of her and that only after they had happened would she take up the teaching; the last lines show her hearing dharma and vowing to end becoming.
links.teaches: The pairing shows that the epic frames its whole middle, from the prison to the debates of Vanji, as a foretold delay, so that this lesson fulfils a prophecy made eighteen kaathais earlier rather than starting a new episode.

links.note: The Ajivika says all gain, loss, pleasure, pain, birth and death are fixed at conception by fate laid down before; the teacher says the chain has no fixed fate (ஊழ்பாடு இன்றி) and runs by conditions that can be reversed.
links.teaches: Kaathai 27 leaves the Ajivika's fixed fate unanswered, and this line supplies the Buddhist reply: the same goods and ills are conditioned links, so cutting a condition can stop them, which fixed fate rules out. The tension depends on reading ஊழ்பாடு as fixed fate.

links.note: The Brahma-vadin says the world is an egg laid by one god; the teacher says the chain is made by no maker and is not a made thing (பண்ணுநர் இன்றிப் பண்ணப் படாதாய்).
links.teaches: The pairing shows that the creator Manimekalai dismissed without argument in Vanji is excluded here by the structure of the doctrine itself, since a chain in which each link supports the next leaves no place for a maker outside it.

links.note: The Sankhya speaker holds the person to be the one eternal awareness that knows all; the teacher says no thing has a self and makes awareness (உணர்வு) a link conditioned by action.
links.teaches: Held together they show where the Buddhist answer to Sankhya lies: not in denying awareness but in making it the third link of a chain, born of action and ceasing with it, so the eternal knower of kaathai 27 is answered three kaathais later.

links.note: The Kural says a joyless birth comes from the confusion that takes what is not real as real; the teacher names ignorance first of twelve links that end in birth and defines it as holding hearsay clear, as that a hare has horns.
links.teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's மருள் can be given a precise epistemic fault, trusting report over what has been established, and that for the Buddhist teacher this confusion reaches birth only through ten links between, which the couplet's direct cause compresses.

gains.a: a Tamil ethical precedent that already makes confusion about the real the cause of birth, so the first link reads as more than a Buddhist technicality
gains.b: a concrete instance of the unreal taken as real, the hare's horn believed on hearsay, where the couplet names no example

links.note: The Kural calls craving the seed that gives unceasing births to all beings; in the chain craving (வேட்கை) gives clinging, karma and birth, but itself arises from feeling and contact and ceases only when ignorance ceases.
links.teaches: Both make craving the seed of birth, but the chain gives the seed its own seed: craving depends on feeling and, eleven steps back, on ignorance, so the Buddhist cure begins with knowledge where the Kural's chapter begins with cutting craving.

gains.a: evidence that the Tamil ethical tradition placed craving, not ignorance, at the root, which shows the chain's order as a doctrinal choice
gains.b: an account of where craving comes from and how it is stopped, which the couplet's image of the seed leaves out

links.note: The Kural says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and delusion perish; the teacher names the same three, in the same order, as the cause of all he has taught and gives a separate remedy for each.
links.teaches: The Kural names the three roots and promises the end of pain but gives no method; the epic, using the same three words, assigns each root its own discipline, contemplation of impermanence for desire, friendliness for anger, hearing and reflection for delusion.

gains.a: the Kural's claim that pain ends wholly when even the names of the three go, a stronger end-state than the remedies alone state
gains.b: a separate practice for each of the three, where the couplet says only that they must perish

links.note: The teacher says bondage and release have their own causes and no one exists to grant them; Tirumular says grace put the soul into bonds and grace gives release.
links.teaches: The two name the same pair, bondage and release, and give opposite answers to who brings them about: the epic denies any giver, and Tirumular makes one grace the giver of both, so the Buddhist and Saiva accounts of release divide exactly at line 251.

gains.a: a named rival position, a giver of both bondage and release, that line 251's denial excludes
gains.b: a counter-position that shows Tirumular's claim that binding itself is grace is the very claim a causal account without a giver rejects

links.note: The teacher's ten bad deeds include killing, theft, lust and lying, as Tirumular's yama does, but the epic sorts them by body, speech and mind and counts coveting, anger and wrong view as deeds, while Tirumular adds sharing food and shunning drink.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two lists of ten show the same core abstentions serving different ends: for the epic they decide the next birth, for Tirumular they are the first step of yoga toward Siva, and only the epic counts states of mind as deeds.

gains.a: a Saiva counterpart showing the same abstentions used as the first limb of yoga rather than as the ledger of rebirth
gains.b: the epic's body, speech and mind sorting, which shows that the yama list has no item for coveting or wrong view

links.note: Naladiyar says craving enters by five gates, body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears, and whoever guards them reaches release; the teacher counts six gates, with the mind among them, and places craving three links after the gates.
links.teaches: The pairing shows two models of the senses: the quatrain makes the five gates the entry of craving and guarding them the path, while the chain adds the mind as a sixth gate and puts contact and feeling between gate and craving, so guarding the gates is not where the chain is cut.

gains.a: an ethical practice of guarding the gates that the chain's definitions do not state
gains.b: the mind as a sixth gate and the steps between sense and craving, which the quatrain's five gates leave out

links.note: The Kural says griefs keep hold of those who keep hold of attachment; the teacher's truths say sorrow is caused by birth and clinging, and release, which is joy, by not clinging.
links.teaches: The Kural's one-verb picture of grip and grief becomes the second truth, and the epic adds its mirror, release as joy caused by not clinging, so the couplet's warning is shown to be half of a four-part formula.

gains.a: a Tamil saying in which the grip one keeps and the grip of sorrow are one act, which the formula's dry causal statement lacks
gains.b: the positive half the couplet omits: that not clinging is the cause of release, named as joy

new_concepts.gloss: dependent arising: the twelve links, each arising with the one before as its support, and their ceasing in reverse
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: சார்பின் தோன்றி (17), தக்க தக்க சார்பின் தோற்றம் (23), பேதைமை சார்வா செய்கை ஆகும் (104)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: ஐந்து வகைக் கந்தம் (33), ஐங்கந்தம் (190)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word: புத்த (3); also வாமன் (13)

source_issues: Line 54: the core's repair of ௌ read as ெள (தெளிதல்) is accepted.
Line 106 spells அரூரு where lines 45, 84, 102, 107, 121, 138, 163, 172 and 179 have அருஉரு; a spelling variant, not a different link.

Lines 45-47 list twelve links ending in தோற்றம், வினைப்பயன், but the reverse chain (lines 127-130) runs கருமத் தொகுதி, தோற்றம், பிறப்பு as separate steps, which gives thirteen; a link may be doubled in the text.
Short lines at 18, 183, 235 and 241 break the akaval line length and may mark loss or a displaced half-line.
Lines 159-169: each time-label stands before its list; read the other way the present links would be future. I have read label-before-list throughout.
